essays.stem: Explain what an operational plan is, how it differs from a strategic (business) plan, and list the main parts it should contain.
essays.modelAnswer: A strategic or business plan sets the long-term direction of the whole business, often for three to five years: what it wants to achieve, its markets and its main goals. An operational plan is shorter term, often for a month, a quarter or a year, and covers one section or team. It sets out how that team will carry out its share of the business plan day to day. For example, if the business plan aims to grow security grille sales by 20%, the workshop's operational plan sets the monthly output, the people and machines needed and how quality will be kept. The main parts are: clear SMART objectives and KPIs; the tasks and who is responsible for each; the timeline; the resources needed, including people, equipment, materials and money; the budget; the risks and contingency plans; how progress will be monitored and reported; and when the plan will be reviewed.
markingPoints: Strategic plan: long-term, whole business
Operational plan: short-term, one section, puts the strategic plan into action
Relevant example linking the two
Parts: objectives and KPIs, tasks and owners, timeline
Parts: resources, budget, risks and contingency, monitoring and review

essays.stem: Describe how a supervisor can consult the team and other stakeholders when helping to prepare an operational plan, and why this matters.
essays.modelAnswer: The supervisor first explains to the team what the business wants to achieve and the draft targets. They can hold a team meeting, talk to people one to one, or use a simple suggestion form, so that quieter members can also give ideas. They ask the team how long tasks really take, what equipment or training they need, and what problems might get in the way. They also speak to other stakeholders: the store clerk about stock levels, suppliers about delivery times, the maintenance person about machine condition, and managers about the budget. They listen, record the ideas and feed them into the plan, then tell people what was used and why some ideas were not. Consultation matters because the people who do the work know the real problems, so the targets are more realistic. It also builds commitment, because people support a plan they helped make, and it finds risks early.
markingPoints: Explains the goals and draft targets to the team
Uses meetings, one-to-one talks or forms
Consults other stakeholders such as stores, suppliers and managers
Records ideas, uses them and gives feedback
Why: realistic targets, commitment, early risk finding

essays.stem: Explain what KPIs are and why they are used. Suggest four suitable KPIs for a welding and fabrication workshop and say how each would be measured.
essays.modelAnswer: Key performance indicators are measures that show how well a team is doing against the goals of the plan. They turn goals into numbers that can be tracked, so everyone can see progress and problems are spotted early. They should be few, clear and easy to measure. For a workshop, a first KPI is on-time delivery: the percentage of jobs delivered by the agreed date, measured from the job records each month. A second is first-time quality: the percentage of welds or items passing inspection without rework, measured from the inspection records. A third is safety: the number of lost-time injuries or reported near misses, measured from the incident log. A fourth is cost: the actual cost of each job compared with the estimate, measured from invoices and time sheets. Others could be machine utilisation or output per week. Each KPI should have a target, and the results should be shown on a chart and discussed with the team.
markingPoints: Defines KPIs as measures of performance against goals
Explains why they are used: tracking and early warning
Four suitable workshop KPIs
How each is measured, from which records
Targets set and results shown and discussed

essays.stem: Describe how a supervisor identifies the resources needed to carry out an operational plan, and how they would ask for extra resources.
essays.modelAnswer: The supervisor starts from the plan's targets, such as the number of items to make each month, and works out what is needed to make them. For people, they work out the hours needed and the skills and qualifications, and compare them with the hours and skills the team has. For equipment, they check that there are enough machines, that they are in good condition and that maintenance is planned. For materials and consumables, they work out the amounts from the output and past use, and set stock levels and order times. For money, they add up the costs into a budget. Where there is a gap, they look first at what can be done with what is there, such as changing shifts or the order of work. If extra resources are still needed, they write a short request to management: what is needed, why, the cost with quotes, the options considered and the benefit, such as more output or less overtime. They follow the business's approval process.
markingPoints: Starts from targets and works out needs
People: hours, skills, qualifications compared with what is available
Equipment, materials and money (budget)
Looks for solutions within current resources first
Written, costed request with reasons and benefits through the approval process

essays.stem: Explain how a supervisor monitors performance against an operational plan, and what they should do when results fall short.
essays.modelAnswer: The supervisor collects information regularly against the plan's KPIs: output figures, job completion dates, inspection results, spending against the budget, hours worked and safety reports. They record it on a progress chart or spreadsheet, so it is easy to compare with the targets, and they walk the workshop to see what is happening. They review the results at set times, such as weekly, and share them with the team. When results fall short, they first find out why, by looking at the facts and talking to the people involved: for example, a machine was broken, materials arrived late, or there was rework. Then they agree corrective action with the team, such as fixing the machine, changing the order of work or extra training. If the problem is outside their authority, they report it to management with the facts and a suggested solution. They record the actions and check that they worked, and update the plan if needed.
markingPoints: Collects data against KPIs regularly from records and observation
Records on a chart or spreadsheet and reviews at set times
Finds the cause of any shortfall from facts and people
Agrees corrective action; reports what is beyond their authority
Records and checks results; updates the plan

essays.stem: Describe how a supervisor identifies and manages risks to an operational plan. Give examples from a fabrication workshop in Jamaica.
essays.modelAnswer: The supervisor lists what could stop the plan being met, with the team's help. Examples are power cuts, a key machine breaking down, late steel deliveries from importers, a skilled welder being off sick, price rises or a storm in the hurricane season. For each risk, they judge how likely it is and how serious the effect would be, often using a risk matrix, so that they can deal with the biggest risks first. Then they plan controls to make the risk less likely or less serious: for example, planned maintenance for machines, ordering steel early and keeping a minimum stock, training a second person in key skills, or having a generator or planning work around scheduled outages. They also write contingency plans for what to do if the risk happens, such as moving work to another machine or securing the workshop before a storm. The risks are written in a risk register, reviewed regularly and updated when things change.
markingPoints: Lists risks with the team
Relevant Jamaican workshop examples
Rates likelihood and consequence
Plans controls and contingency plans
Risk register reviewed and updated

essays.stem: Explain how a supervisor can support the recruitment, induction and development of staff needed to carry out an operational plan.
essays.modelAnswer: From the plan, the supervisor works out how many people and which skills are needed, and compares this with the team. If there is a gap, they help write the job description and the skills and qualifications needed, for example a welder qualified in pipe welding. They may help shortlist and interview applicants, following the business's fair recruitment policy and asking the same job-related questions of each candidate. When a new person starts, the supervisor makes sure they get a full induction: safety rules, PPE, emergency procedures, the team, the job and the policies. They pair the new person with an experienced worker at first. For development, the supervisor checks the skills the plan needs against each person's skills, and arranges training, coaching or practice, for example aluminium welding for a new contract. They keep training records and review progress with each person. This makes sure the team can meet the plan safely and to the right quality.
markingPoints: Identifies the people and skills needed from the plan
Helps write job needs and takes part in fair selection
Ensures a full induction and buddy support
Identifies training needs and arranges training or coaching
Keeps training records and reviews progress

essays.stem: Explain how a supervisor helps prepare and control a budget for a workshop's operational plan.
essays.modelAnswer: To prepare the budget, the supervisor uses the plan's workload and past records to estimate the costs for the period: materials, consumables such as wire, gas and discs, labour hours and overtime, maintenance, equipment hire and small tools. They get prices from suppliers and check them with the purchasing person. They set out the figures by month and by cost heading, add a small contingency, and agree the budget with their manager. To control it, they compare the actual spending with the budget each month, using the invoices and time sheets. They work out the variance for each heading, in J$ and as a percentage. Where spending is over budget, they find out why, such as wasted material, price rises or extra overtime, and take action, such as reducing waste or re-planning the work. If the budget cannot be met, they tell their manager early, with reasons. They keep accurate records and follow the business's rules for approving spending.
markingPoints: Uses workload and past records to estimate costs by heading
Gets prices; sets out by month; agrees with the manager
Compares actual with budget monthly and works out variances
Finds reasons and takes action on overspending
Reports early; keeps records; follows approval rules

essays.stem: Describe how a supervisor can encourage continuous improvement while carrying out an operational plan. Use a workshop example.
essays.modelAnswer: Continuous improvement means always looking for small, practical ways to do the work better, safer, faster or with less waste. The supervisor encourages the team to suggest ideas, for example at the end of the daily meeting or with a suggestion box, and treats every idea with respect. They use the plan's KPIs to spot where improvement is most needed, such as a high rate of rework on gate hinges. They can use a simple Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle. For example, a welder suggests a jig to hold hinges in place. The team plans a trial, makes the jig and uses it on the next ten gates, checks the time and the rework rate against before, and if it works, the jig becomes standard practice and the plan is updated. The supervisor thanks the person who suggested it and shares the result. They record improvements and report them to management, because small savings across many jobs add up.
markingPoints: Defines continuous improvement
Encourages and respects ideas from the team
Uses KPIs to find where to improve
Uses a trial cycle such as PDCA with a workshop example
Recognises contributions; records, shares and updates the plan

essays.stem: Describe what a supervisor should include in a monthly report on progress against the operational plan, and how to make it clear and useful.
essays.modelAnswer: The report should start with a short summary: whether the team is on track, and the main points. It should show each KPI against its target for the month, such as output, on-time delivery, first-time quality, safety and cost. It should show the budget against actual spending, with the variances. It should explain the reasons for any shortfall and the actions taken or planned, with who is responsible and by when. It should note any risks that are growing, resource needs, staffing changes or training given. It should include improvements made and good work by the team. To make it clear, the supervisor should use plain words, short headings and simple charts or tables with the target shown, and keep it to one or two pages. Figures must be accurate and honest, even when results are poor, because management needs the true picture to make decisions. The report should be dated, sent on time and kept on file.
markingPoints: Summary of whether the plan is on track
KPIs and budget against targets with variances
Reasons for shortfalls and actions with owners and dates
Risks, resources, staffing and improvements
Clear format with charts; accurate, honest, on time and filed

practical1.title: Draft an operational plan for a month's production in the welding workshop
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your team a planning brief: for example, the Centre's workshop has an order for 20 steel security grilles and 6 gates, to be delivered within one month, with the staff, machines, stock levels and costs given. As a team, draft an operational plan for the month on the planning forms. First, agree who leads each part. The plan must include: three SMART objectives; at least four KPIs with targets; the tasks, who is responsible and a week-by-week timeline (a bar chart); the resources needed (people and hours, machines, materials and consumables) compared with what is available, with any gap and how you would close it; a simple budget by cost heading; and a risk table with at least four risks, their rating, controls and contingency plans. Then make a poster that shows the plan on one page for the team. Each member drafts at least one part and checks another member's part. Present the plan to the assessor in 10 minutes, with each member speaking. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the plan, the poster and the presentation are finished.
materials: Planning brief from the assessor (order, staff, machines, stock and costs)
Operational plan forms: objectives and KPIs, task and timeline, resources, budget, risk table
Chart paper, markers and rulers for the poster
Calculators; a computer with a spreadsheet may be used
photos: The team reading the brief and sharing out the parts
The SMART objectives and KPIs form
The task list and bar chart timeline
The resources and budget forms with the gap worked out
The one-page poster of the plan
The team presenting to the assessor
checklist: Wrote SMART objectives and measurable KPIs with targets
Listed tasks with owners and a realistic timeline
Worked out the resources needed and compared them with what is available
Prepared a budget with correct calculations
Identified risks, rated them and set controls and contingency plans
Checked another member's part and helped correct it
Spoke clearly about their part in the presentation
Worked well with others and kept to time
safety: Keep bags and cables out of walkways in the classroom
Sit at the computer with good posture and take short breaks
Use markers and any spray adhesive for the poster with ventilation

practical2.title: Monitor results against the plan, write a variance report and present it to management (role play)
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your team the operational plan for a workshop and the actual results for the first month: output, delivery dates, inspection results, hours worked, spending by cost heading and incidents. As a team, compare the results with the plan. Work out each variance in units or J$ and as a percentage, show the KPIs on a simple chart with the target line, and pick out where the plan is behind. For each shortfall, use a problem-solving method (for example the 5 whys) to suggest a likely cause from the information given, and agree a corrective action with an owner and a date. Write a one- to two-page monthly report. Then role-play a meeting with management: two members present the report, one member plays the manager (using the assessor's role card) and asks questions or asks for extra resources to be justified, and the others answer. Swap roles so every member presents or answers at least once. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the report and the meeting notes are finished.
materials: The operational plan and the month's actual results from the assessor
Variance sheets, chart paper or a computer with a spreadsheet
Report template and meeting notes sheet
Manager role card from the assessor
photos: The variance sheet with the calculations
The KPI chart with the target line
The problem-solving notes for a shortfall
The corrective action list with owners and dates
The role-play meeting with management in progress
checklist: Worked out variances in units or J$ and as percentages correctly
Showed KPIs clearly on a chart against the targets
Found likely causes using a clear method
Agreed realistic corrective actions with owners and dates
Helped write an accurate, clear and honest report
Presented or answered questions clearly and politely
Justified any request for resources with figures
Worked well with others and kept to time
safety: Keep bags and cables out of walkways
Sit at the computer with good posture and take short breaks
Keep the role play respectful and professional
